title: Given an array that may contain duplicates, return all unique subsets using backtracking.
shortTitle: Subsets II (with duplicates): sort then skip duplicates
keyPoints: Sort the array so equal values are adjacent, enabling a simple skip condition for duplicates.
At each recursion level, skip an element if its index is beyond the level's start and it equals the previous element.
The condition i > start is crucial: it allows the first occurrence to be chosen while blocking a second identical choice at the same level.
Record the current path at every entry point to capture all subset sizes, including the empty set.
Worst-case time is O(n times 2 to the n) for all-distinct elements, reduced when duplicates prune branches.
The same skip-same-level-duplicate pattern reappears in Combination Sum II and Permutations II.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, then at each level skip a value equal to its predecessor to drop duplicate subsets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Subsets II** – generate all unique subsets (the power set) from an array that may contain duplicates.
- **Sort first** – places equal values adjacent so duplicates can be detected by comparing neighbors.
- **Skip guard** – `if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue` suppresses duplicate subsets at each decision level.
- **i > start** – allows the first occurrence to be chosen and recursed into, blocking only the second identical choice at the same level.
- **Time** – O(n * 2^n) worst case for all-distinct elements.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has add-on vouchers where some are identical. Two identical vouchers should not produce two different-looking-but-equal promotional packages. By lining up identical vouchers and, at each decision point, using an identical voucher only once as the "first" choice, you avoid listing the same package twice.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input: [100, 200, 200] (after sort)

  Recursion tree with skip:
  ┌─ [] (record)
  │
  ├─ [100] (record)
  │   ├─ [100, 200] (record)     i=1
  │   │   └─ [100, 200, 200] (record) i=2
  │   └─ [100, 200] SKIP         i=2, i>start && 200==200
  │
  ├─ [200] (record)              i=1 (first 200)
  │   └─ [200, 200] (record)     i=2
  │
  └─ [200] SKIP                  i=2, i>start=0? NO, i>0? YES
          but i > start (start=0), 200==200 --> SKIP

  Output: [], [100], [100,200], [100,200,200], [200], [200,200]
  (6 unique subsets, no duplicates)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets II extends the power-set backtracking to inputs that contain duplicates, where the goal is every distinct subset with no repeats in the output. The two essential moves are sorting the array first so equal values are adjacent, and then adding a guard inside the loop that skips an element when its index is beyond the current level's start and it equals the previous element.

The condition `i > start` is what makes it correct: the first occurrence of a duplicate value at a level is allowed and recursed into, where the duplicate can legitimately extend the path deeper, but a second identical choice at the same level is blocked because it would produce an already-generated subset. Using `i > 0` instead would skip too aggressively and miss valid subsets like `[200, 200]`.

The worst-case cost is still O(n times 2^n) for all-distinct elements, but duplicates prune branches. The same skip-same-level-duplicate pattern reappears in Combination Sum II and Permutations II, so I treat it as one reusable technique rather than three separate tricks.

In my project at National Bank of India, marketing built promotional bundles from a voucher pool that contained identical vouchers and needed every distinct bundle listed once. This sorted, skip-same-level-duplicate pattern produced clean unique bundles without any post-processing deduplication.

Remember one sentence: sort the array, then skip any element at a recursion level whose index exceeds the level start and whose value equals the previous element, to generate all unique subsets.
